title: Idempotency & Ledger
description: Implement idempotency keys for at-most-once payment processing, double-entry bookkeeping, T+1 reconciliation, and learn from Stripe's idempotency implementation.

segments.text: The nightmare scenario: a network timeout during payment processing. The client retries. Did the first request succeed? If yes, the customer is charged twice. If you don't retry, the payment might be lost. Stripe handles this with idempotency keys — every payment request includes a UUID. If the server sees the same UUID again, it returns the original response.

The idempotency key is a client-generated UUID sent in the Idempotency-Key header. The server stores it with the response. On retry, the server looks up the key — if it exists and the request completed, return the stored response. If it exists but is still processing, return 409 Conflict. Stripe retains idempotency keys for twenty-four hours.

Idempotency gives you at-most-once processing. Combined with retries, you get effectively-exactly-once. The key implementation detail: the idempotency check and the payment processing must be in the same database transaction. Otherwise, a crash between the check and the processing creates a window for duplicates.

Double-entry bookkeeping is the foundation of financial systems. Every transaction has two entries: a debit from one account and a credit to another. Customer pays one hundred dollars: debit customer wallet one hundred, credit merchant account one hundred. The sum of all debits must equal the sum of all credits — always. If they don't, you have a bug.

The ledger is an append-only log of all financial transactions. Never update or delete entries — only add new correcting entries. A refund isn't deleting the original charge — it's a new entry: debit merchant one hundred, credit customer one hundred. This audit trail is legally required and provides complete transaction history for dispute resolution.

Your payment system processed ten million transactions today. The ledger shows total debits don't match total credits — they're off by three hundred forty-seven dollars. How do you find and fix the discrepancy?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you investigate a $347 discrepancy in 10M daily transactions? What's your reconciliation approach?

segments.text: Reconciliation compares your internal ledger with external systems — bank statements, payment processor records, partner reports. T-plus-one settlement means you reconcile yesterday's transactions today. Automated reconciliation matches ninety-nine percent of transactions. The remaining one percent — mismatches, missing records, timing differences — requires manual investigation.

Stripe's idempotency implementation uses a state machine for each idempotency key: started, executing, finished, or errored. They use database row locks to prevent concurrent execution of the same key. If the server crashes during execution, a background worker detects stuck 'executing' keys after a timeout and marks them for retry.

Never use floating-point for money. Ever. IEEE 754 floating point can't represent zero point one exactly. After a million operations, rounding errors accumulate into real money discrepancies. Use integer cents — one hundred for one dollar. Or use decimal types with fixed precision. Stripe stores all amounts in the smallest currency unit — cents for USD, yen for JPY.

Design the ledger and idempotency system for a payment platform processing one million transactions per day across twelve currencies. What's your data model, consistency guarantees, and reconciliation strategy?
segments.thought_prompt: Design a payment ledger for 1M daily transactions across 12 currencies with full reconciliation.

segments.text: Payment systems require paranoid engineering. Idempotency keys prevent double charges, double-entry bookkeeping ensures every cent is accounted for, append-only ledgers provide audit trails, T-plus-one reconciliation catches discrepancies, and integer arithmetic prevents floating-point errors. In payments, correctness is more important than performance. Get the money right.
